content: In the United States, influenza epidemics typically occur during the winter months and have been associated with an average of approximately 36,000 deaths annually between 1990 and 1999. Influenza viruses can cause illness across all age groups, with the highest infection rates observed among children. However, the most severe illnesses and deaths occur among individuals aged 65 years and older, children under 2 years of age, and individuals of any age with underlying medical conditions that increase their risk of complications from influenza. Influenza vaccination is the primary method for preventing influenza and its severe complications. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommends annual influenza vaccination for specific groups, including individuals at high risk for influenza-related complications, such as children aged 6–59 months, pregnant women, individuals aged 50 years and older, and those with chronic medical conditions. Vaccination is also recommended for individuals who live with or care for high-risk individuals, including household contacts and healthcare workers. Vaccination can prevent hospitalizations and deaths among high-risk individuals and reduce influenza-related respiratory illnesses, physician visits, otitis media in children, and work absenteeism in adults. Despite increased vaccination rates during the 1990s, further improvements are needed, particularly among individuals aged 65 years and older, children aged 6–23 months, and healthcare workers. Strategies to improve vaccination coverage include reminder/recall systems and standing orders programs. While vaccination remains the cornerstone of influenza control, antiviral medications are also important adjuncts. However, due to widespread resistance of influenza A viruses to amantadine and rimantadine, these medications are no longer recommended for treatment or chemoprophylaxis. Instead, oseltamivir or zanamivir may be prescribed when antiviral treatment is indicated. Influenza A and B viruses are responsible for epidemic human disease. Influenza A viruses are further categorized into subtypes based on surface antigens, hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA), while influenza B viruses are not subtyped. Since 1977, influenza A (H1N1), A (H3N2), and B viruses have circulated globally. Antigenic drift, resulting from point mutations during viral replication, leads to the emergence of new strains and necessitates annual updates to the influenza vaccine. Antigenic shifts, which occur less frequently, can result in novel influenza viruses with pandemic potential. Influenza is primarily transmitted via respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing. The incubation period is typically 1–4 days, with an average of 2 days. Adults are infectious from the day before symptom onset to approximately 5 days after illness onset, while children can remain infectious for more than 10 days. Severely immunocompromised individuals may shed the virus for weeks or months. Uncomplicated influenza illness usually resolves within 3–7 days, although cough and malaise may persist for more than 2 weeks. Complications, such as secondary bacterial pneumonia, primary influenza viral pneumonia, or co-infections with other pathogens, can occur, particularly in individuals with underlying medical conditions. Influenza virus infection has also been associated with rare complications, including encephalopathy, transverse myelitis, myocarditis, pericarditis, and Reye syndrome. The risk of complications, hospitalizations, and deaths from influenza is higher among individuals aged 65 years and older, young children, and those with underlying health conditions. During seasonal influenza epidemics from 1979–1980 through 2000–2001, an average of approximately 226,000 influenza-related hospitalizations occurred annually in the United States, with 63% of these hospitalizations among individuals aged 65 years and older. Influenza-related deaths are most common among older adults, accounting for more than 90% of deaths attributed to pneumonia and influenza. Annual vaccination is the primary strategy for reducing the impact of influenza. Both inactivated influenza vaccines (IIV) and live attenuated influenza vaccines (LAIV) are available in the United States. Vaccination coverage can be increased by offering vaccines during routine healthcare visits, hospitalizations, and at community locations such as pharmacies and workplaces. Vaccination of healthcare workers and individuals in close contact with high-risk individuals can reduce transmission and subsequent complications. Inactivated influenza vaccines contain killed viruses and are administered intramuscularly, while LAIV contains live, attenuated viruses and is administered intranasally. LAIV is approved for healthy individuals aged 5–49 years, whereas IIV is approved for individuals aged 6 months and older, including those with chronic medical conditions. Both vaccines are effective, but their efficacy depends on factors such as the recipient's age, immune status, and the match between vaccine and circulating virus strains. Studies have demonstrated that influenza vaccination is effective in preventing illness, reducing hospitalizations, and decreasing work absenteeism. Among healthy adults aged less than 65 years, vaccination typically prevents influenza illness in approximately 70%–90% of cases when vaccine and circulating viruses are well-matched. Among older adults, vaccination is 30%–70% effective in preventing hospitalizations for pneumonia and influenza and 50%–60% effective in preventing influenza-related deaths in nursing home residents. The immunogenicity of LAIV has been assessed in multiple studies, demonstrating high efficacy in preventing culture-confirmed influenza among children and healthy adults. LAIV has also been associated with reductions in febrile otitis media and febrile illnesses. However, the protective mechanisms induced by LAIV are not fully understood and appear to involve both serum and nasal secretory antibodies. In summary, annual influenza vaccination is essential for preventing influenza and its complications, particularly among high-risk populations. Both IIV and LAIV are effective options, with specific recommendations based on age and health status. Antiviral medications serve as important adjuncts to vaccination but are not substitutes for annual immunization.
